The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education has transformed language learning practices, particularly through the emergence of ChatGPT as an intelligent conversational tool. For Health Administration students, English grammar plays a crucial role in developing professional communication skills required for administrative documentation, healthcare reporting, policy writing, and international collaboration. ChatGPT offers opportunities to enhance grammar learning through interactive explanations, personalized feedback, and autonomous learning experiences tailored to learners' academic and professional needs. However, its implementation also raises pedagogical and ethical concerns regarding response accuracy, learner dependence, and academic integrity. This critical literature review discusses the theoretical foundations of English grammar learning for Health Administration students, explores the educational potential of ChatGPT, critically examines its pedagogical implications, and identifies challenges and future directions for AI-assisted grammar instruction.

Learning environment is one of the most crucial key factors for Mathematics-learning. Educational stake-holders should be promoted to adapt the innovation techniques by every educational institutions’ policy makers. Stable Falsehoods in Large Language Models: A Consistency-Based Approach to Hallucination Analysis Creators Niall Devlin (Concept Originator) Affiliation (if desired): Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council Service Director, Education & Inclusion Publication Date Use the date you submit/publish on Zenodo. Resource Type Publication → Preprint (recommended) Alternatively: Report (if you consider it a working paper) Software (for the prototype separately) Description / Abstract Most Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation frameworks focus primarily on factual correctness. This paper proposes an alternative perspective by examining the interaction between correctness and consistency. It introduces the concept of the Stable Falsehood: a response pattern in which a model repeatedly generates the same incorrect answer across multiple independent samples. The framework evaluates LLM behaviour using repeated fresh-context sampling and measures agreement, accuracy, entropy, and semantic similarity as separate dimensions. By analysing the relationship between correctness and consistency, the methodology classifies responses into behavioural categories including Stable Correct, Stable Falsehood, Variable Correct, Variable False, and Chaotic. The accompanying prototype, the Confabulation Variance Test (Research Edition v4), demonstrates practical implementation of the methodology through repeated sampling, statistical analysis, entropy measurement, and behavioural classification. The principal contribution is the systematic treatment of consistency and correctness as independent dimensions whose interaction reveals distinct forms of model reliability. The work argues that a model which is consistently wrong may represent a different and potentially more significant reliability challenge than a model which is inconsistently wrong. Beyond Cheating: Preparing Students and Institutions for Responsible Generative AI Use in Higher Education Author: Vanzal Dhliwayo Institution: Southeast New Mexico College Abstract The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, CoPilot and many more has generated both excitement and concern across higher education. Much of the early institutional conversation centered on whether students would use systems such as ChatGPT to complete assignments, quizzes, examinations, and other academic work. Although these concerns are legitimate, framing generative AI primarily as a cheating problem overlooks its considerable educational potential. Research has shown that artificial intelligence technologies have the potential to revolutionize education than anything else (Harry, et al.,2023). There are many things these tools can do. Students can use them to clarify difficult concepts, generate practice questions, organize notes, receive formative feedback, brainstorm ideas, and examine alternative explanations. Educators can use it to develop examples, improve instructional materials, create formative assessments, differentiate explanations, prepare rubrics, and revise course materials. It has also been shown by recent research that the educational effects of generative AI depend less on the mere presence of the technology than on how instructors design learning experiences around it. One of the meta-analysis' research projects concluded that artificial intelligence tools have a positive effect on student's academic performance (Liu et al., 2025), while some other publications show a concern in continuing gaps in institutional guidance, professional development, automated online learning, and assessment strategy (Fan et al., 2026; Baggia et al., 2026). In this short paper I will present a practice-oriented review of research on artificial technology tools in higher education and propose a good framework for integrating those tools while protecting academic integrity. Throughout the paper I will pay more attention to AI literacy, assessment design, transparency, equity, privacy, human oversight, and syllabus development. In this paper I argue that universities and colleges need to move away from a simple binary of "AI allowed" versus "AI prohibited" and instead specify appropriate AI use according to the learning objectives of individual assignments. The proposed framework has five parts: Course outcomes first; Label AI permissions; Educate for AI literacy; Assess learning processes; and Review risks, equity, and policy. I also provided one adaptable syllabus template. My conclusion is that instead of just labeling generative AI as a cheating tool, institutions need to protect academic integrity by teaching students how to use AI responsibly, redesigning assessments to reveal students' thinking, and establishing clear expectations rather than relying predominantly on prohibition or automated AI detection.
